lead: A micro sensor is built on a silicon wafer by integrated-circuit steps. Micromachining etches a thin diaphragm, beam or channel a few micrometres thick. Pressure, force or flow bends it, and piezoresistors, a capacitor or a heater turns the bending into a voltage. The sensor fits in a few square millimetres. Phone barometers, tyre pressure monitors, blood-pressure cuffs and ventilator flow tubes use these.
prereq: You need strain gauges, the gauge factor and load cells from resistive transducers; capacitive transducers and bridge circuits; and the seismic accelerometer.

blocks.text: Start with a silicon wafer and etch a cavity into the back until a thin square or circular diaphragm is left, typically 5 to 25 µm thick. The thick rim clamps the diaphragm, so the largest stress sits at the clamped edge, not the centre. A sealed vacuum underneath gives an absolute sensor; an open hole gives a gauge sensor reading the difference of two pressures.

Four resistors are ion-implanted into the surface at the edge. Two run across the edge, along the main stress, and two run parallel to it. In p-type silicon the piezoresistive coefficient along the stress and the one across it have opposite signs, so the first pair rises in resistance and the second pair falls by about the same amount. Strain ε is the fractional change in length (m/m). Resistance change follows gauge factor G: a silicon piezoresistor has G between about 100 and 200, while a metal foil gauge has G near 2. The same strain therefore gives 50 to 100 times more signal.

blocks.where: ΔR is the change in resistance (Ω), R is the unstrained resistance (Ω), G is the gauge factor (dimensionless) and ε is the strain (m/m).

blocks.text: The four resistors form a full Wheatstone bridge fed from supply V<sub>s</sub>. Opposite arms shift oppositely, so the four-active bridge gives four times the output of a single active gauge and cancels common temperature drift. A typical part is quoted in millivolts per volt supply per bar, for example 30 mV at 5 V and 1 bar, which is 6 mV/V/bar; commercial parts run from about 5 to 20 mV/V/bar at full-scale pressure. The disposable blood-pressure transducer on a patient's arterial line is this sensor, built to a standard sensitivity of 5 µV per volt per mmHg: at 5 V excitation a pressure of 120 mmHg gives 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 5 × 120 = 3.0 mV. Catheter-tip and implanted versions read pressure inside the heart or skull. An amplifier and ADC follow the bridge, as 30 mV is too small to digitise directly.

Keep deflection below about one fifth of the diaphragm thickness. Beyond that the diaphragm stiffens, the output bends away from a straight line, and the part is sold with a linearity error stated as a percentage of full scale.

Here the diaphragm is one plate of a capacitor, and a fixed plate sits a small gap behind it, sealed in vacuum. The gap is 1 to 2 µm and the plates overlap over an area A of about a square millimetre.

blocks.where: C is the capacitance (F), ε is the permittivity of the gas in the gap (F/m, about 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m for air or vacuum), A is the overlap area (m²) and d is the gap (m).

blocks.text: Differentiating gives ΔC/C ≈ −Δd/d for small movement: a 1 % squeeze of the gap gives a 1 % rise in capacitance. The 1/d law is nonlinear, so the readout must linearise it, either by forcing the diaphragm back with electrostatic feedback or by letting it touch the backplate over part of the range, flattening the curve.

Reading uses an AC bridge, a charge amplifier, or most often a switched-capacitor circuit. Switches charge the sensor capacitor and a fixed reference capacitor, then dump both charges into an integrator. The output is proportional to C<sub>sensor</sub>/C<sub>ref</sub>, so it does not drift with supply or temperature. The sensing node is held at a virtual ground, so stray capacitance to ground carries no signal current, and a guard ring at the same potential blocks surface leakage.

Compared with the piezoresistive type, the capacitive sensor draws almost no DC current, is more linear after feedback, and resolves a few pascal, suiting barometers, altimeters and microphones. Its weaknesses are stray capacitance, electromagnetic interference and package stress, needing shielding and careful mounting.

sections.h3: Force, tactile and flow micro sensors

blocks.text: Put a polymer bump on a thin membrane or cantilever, and the structure measures contact force. An array of such cells under a rubber pad gives a map of force over the contact area, a tactile image. Normal force is read from capacitance between the plates; a pair of cells, one on each side of a bump, gives the shear direction as the bump shifts sideways. Robot grippers, touch panels and Braille displays use this.

For flow, the common micro sensor is a thermal anemometer. A heater sits on a thin membrane, with a thermopile upstream and another downstream. A thermopile is many thermocouples in series, giving a few millivolts without excitation. With no flow, heat spreads equally and both thermopiles see the same temperature. With flow, heat is swept downstream, the downstream thermopile gets hotter, and the difference voltage rises with mass flow but not linearly: near linear at very low flow, flattening at higher flow, so the part uses a calibration look-up table; the sign gives direction. Driving the heater at constant temperature above ambient widens the range.

A second type is the differential-pressure micro flow sensor. A micromachined orifice or narrow channel is etched in the wafer, and the pressure drop across it is read by a diaphragm sensor like the one above. For smooth laminar flow the drop is linear, ΔP = R<sub>h</sub>·Q, so Q = ΔP/R<sub>h</sub>, where Q is volume flow (m³/s) and R<sub>h</sub> is hydraulic resistance (Pa·s/m³). R<sub>h</sub> depends on viscosity, so the part is calibrated for one gas or liquid. Gas meters and drug-delivery pumps use it because it has no moving parts.

Coriolis and ultrasonic micro flow sensors exist; their working is only named here. Thermal micro flow sensors sit in ventilators and spirometers to measure breath flow, and in infusion pumps to watch drug flow. Position and speed micro sensors use Hall elements and optical encoder gratings on the same wafer. Acceleration and temperature micro sensors come from the same diaphragm and beam process.

examples.question: A piezoresistive pressure sensor has a gauge factor G = 120 and a diaphragm strain of 2 × 10⁻⁴ at full scale. Each resistor is 5 kΩ and the bridge is supplied with 5 V. Find the relative resistance change, the change in each resistance, and the bridge output when only one gauge is active.
steps: One active gauge gives a quarter of the full-bridge output: V₀ ≈ V<sub>s</sub>·(ΔR/R)/4 = 5 V × 0.024/4 = 0.03 V.
Convert: 0.03 V = 30 mV. Four active gauges give 4 × 30 = 120 mV.
examples.answer: Relative change 0.024; each resistance changes by 120 Ω; one active gauge gives 0.03 V (30 mV).
examples.check:
G = 120.0
eps = 2e-4
R = 5000.0
Vs = 5.0
dR_over_R = G * eps
dR = dR_over_R * R
V0 = Vs * dR_over_R / 4
print(dR_over_R)
print(dR)
print(V0)

examples.question: A capacitive pressure sensor has plates of overlap area 1.0 mm² separated by a 2.0 µm vacuum gap. Under pressure the gap closes to 1.9 µm. Find the capacitance before and after, the change, and compare the exact percentage change with the small-change estimate.
steps: ΔC = 4.660 − 4.427 = 0.233 pF. Exact change: 0.233 / 4.427 = 5.26 %; the estimate Δd/d gives 5.0 %.
Check the scale: 0.233 pF is smaller than the capacitance of a few centimetres of cable, which is why the readout circuit sits on the same chip or right beside it.
examples.answer: C rises from 4.427 pF to 4.660 pF, a change of 0.233 pF or 5.26 % (5.0 % by the small-change estimate).
examples.check:
e0 = 8.854e-12
A = 1.0e-6
C1 = e0 * A / 2.0e-6
C2 = e0 * A / 1.9e-6
print(round(C1 * 1e12, 3))
print(round(C2 * 1e12, 3))
print(round((C2 - C1) * 1e12, 3))
print(round((C2 / C1 - 1) * 100, 2))

traps: Dropping the factor 4. One active gauge gives V<sub>s</sub>·(ΔR/R)/4; four give V<sub>s</sub>·(ΔR/R). Using full-bridge value for one gauge is the commonest lost mark.
Putting resistors at the centre. A clamped plate has almost no radial stress there; maximum bending stress is at the edge.
Mixing pressure units. 1 bar = 100 kPa = 14.5 psi, so 10 mV/V/bar ≈ 0.69 mV/V/psi; convert before comparing data sheets.

quiz.q: State typical gauge factors for a silicon piezoresistor and a metal foil gauge.
Why place the four piezoresistors at the clamped edge, not the centre?
quiz.a: The rim clamps the plate, so bending stress is greatest at the edge and near zero at the centre. Resistance change follows strain, so edge placement gives the largest signal.

quiz.q: Why wire all four piezoresistors as a full bridge instead of one active gauge?
quiz.a: Output is four times larger, and common temperature drift cancels because opposite arms shift oppositely.

quiz.q: A capacitive pressure sensor has a 2.0 µm gap. Pressure reduces it to 1.9 µm. Find the percentage change in capacitance.
quiz.a: Δd = 0.1 µm. C is proportional to 1/d, so C₂/C₁ = d₁/d₂ = 2.0/1.9 = 1.0526: the capacitance rises by 5.26 %. The small-change estimate Δd/d = 0.1/2.0 = 5 % is close because the squeeze is small.

quiz.q: A piezoresistive sensor has sensitivity 8 mV/V/bar and supply 5 V. Output at 0.4 bar?
Why does switched-capacitor readout reject stray capacitance to ground better than a plain AC bridge?
quiz.a: The sensor plate sits at a virtual ground, so voltage across any stray capacitance to ground is nearly zero and no signal current flows into it. A guard ring at the same potential intercepts surface leakage.

quiz.q: A differential-pressure micro flow sensor calibrated for air is used on water. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: For laminar flow Q = ΔP/R<sub>h</sub>, and R<sub>h</sub> depends on viscosity. Water is far more viscous than air, so the same flow gives a much larger pressure drop. The stored calibration and laminar range no longer hold.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production micro sensors come from foundries running deep reactive ion etching and wafer bonding; aluminium nitride films build micromachined ultrasonic transducers. Search bulk micromachining and the Bosch process.
